en.title: iOS 27 and iPadOS 27: A Summary of VoiceOver and Braille Issues and Improvements
en.summary: iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 were released to the public on Monday, September 14, 2026. This post contains a summary of new bugs and fixes impacting VoiceOver and Braille support that the AppleVis Editorial Team has independently validated during our use and testing of these releases. The information contained in this post is compiled from our own use and testing of iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 during the beta period from June to September 2026; as well as from validated reports submitted by others through our Community Bug Program and shared on the AppleVis Forum. Our sincere appreciation goes to everyone who so generously took the time to share their findings with us. At the outset, we need to state explicitly that the bug list contained in this post is not definitive and that our assessments are not infallible. While we are confident in the presence of the issues discussed in this post, there are many other reports shared on the AppleVis Forum by members of our community that we have not been able to independently replicate with the available information. Many of these reports represented use cases that are different from those of our team; and a small number were issues that, despite understanding how to reproduce them, we did not get the same results. We say all of this so that readers understand the limits of our own testing, and that others' experiences may be different from ours. An issue not being present in our bug list does not mean the issue does not exist; it simply means that we are either unaware of or unable to reproduce it. As is our routine practice, each bug in this post has been given a severity rating. These ratings are based upon what we believe to be the implications for accessing and using features and functionality for the average user; the level of impact on the overall user experience; and whether or not there is an effective workaround for the issue. However, as these ratings are subjective to an extent, it is very possible that they may not reflect your own opinion or use case. With this in mind, we strongly recommend reading this full post and any replies before updating to iOS 27 and iPadOS 27; as we believe this will help you make an informed decision on whether to install the software at the current time or to wait for a future release. We also strongly recommend that you read this Megathread about the iOS 27 RC , as it contains a wealth of community reports about and experiences with the Release Candidate version of the software. Some issues listed in this post and on the Forum may manifest only under specific conditions; this is all the more likely as software continues to add more features and the number of devices, available configurations, and use cases in Apple's ecosystem continues to grow. You likely will not experience every bug that we list, and you likely will not agree with every severity rating for the bugs that you do experience. While we wish it were otherwise, this is to be expected. And as is the nature with all software, it is also likely that you will encounter issues that are not reported in this post. To ensure the information in this post is as complete and accurate as possible, we would appreciate input from those who have installed iOS 27 or iPadOS 27. Please confirm if you are encountering the same problems listed or if you have found workarounds. Please also let us know about any additional issues not mentioned here. Of course, it is even more important that you report any new bugs directly to Apple - they are already aware of the ones listed in this post. For an explanation of why and how to report bugs to Apple, see this post. With all of the preamble out of the way, below are the new bugs for VoiceOver and Braille users which members of the AppleVis Editorial Team have personally experienced and believe to be present in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27: A Major Change to VoiceOver's Audio Profile In iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, there is a significant change in the sound profile of VoiceOver when the device's internal speaker is used. When compared to iOS 26, VoiceOver audio in iOS 27 has significantly less bass, particularly at lower volume levels. The resulting sound might best be described as 'neutral' or 'flat', with significantly less of the low-end emphasis and other processing that has characterized VoiceOver audio in recent versions of iOS/iPadOS. If you have not yet upgraded to iOS 27, we believe that you can get a reasonable approximation of how VoiceOver will sound on your device by making a phone call, putting the call on speaker, and then using VoiceOver to navigate around the screen; as the flatter, more neutral sound profile that VoiceOver uses during a phone call sounds very similar to what we are hearing in iOS 27. At the time of publication, we do not know whether the change to VoiceOver's sound profile is expected behavior; thus, we are not including it in our bug list. Nevertheless, we feel that users should be aware of this change before upgrading. If we receive additional information, we will update this post accordingly. Serious Bugs When the state of an item changes or the screen updates, VoiceOver does not always recognize/speak the information. This issue has many manifestations, including (but not limited to): When waking the device, VoiceOver may speak the time the device was last woken rather than the current time; When information updates onscreen (such as the status of an operation in an app), VoiceOver may not speak it right away and instead speak the previously displayed text. There is no known workaround, though VoiceOver will eventually speak the updated information if focus is moved off of and back onto the impacted element enough times. The VoiceOver Per-Voice Equalizer (a feature that allows one to customize certain frequency/tonal characteristics of a voice) does not work. There is no known workaround. If you rely on the per-voice Equalizer, we recommend that you do not install iOS/iPadOS 27 until this issue is resolved. The VoiceOver Pronunciation Dictionary does not work reliably, with custom pronunciations often not being obeyed by VoiceOver. There is no known workaround. If you rely on the Pronunciation Dictionary, we recommend that you do not install iOS/iPadOS 27 until this issue is resolved. If an external audio device is connected, VoiceOver speech does not work when playing audio in Safari. Pausing the audio causes it to start working again. Sometimes, when reading text, VoiceOver stops speaking and does not resume on its own. This issue does not occur all of the time. When it does occur, speech will stop mid-sentence (and sometimes even mid-word). Touching the screen or performing a touch gesture (like a one-finger swipe left or right) restores speech, and the user can then refocus VoiceOver on the impacted element. In iOS 27's new Recovery Menu, there is no spoken feedback in Diagnostics Mode, rendering this option completely inaccessible. There is no known workaround to make Diagnostics Mode itself usable. If you do manage to accidentally get your device into Diagnostics Mode, our experience is that the device will restart into normal operation after approximately five to ten minutes of inactivity. Moderate Bugs On some devices, Sound Curtain and Touch Curtain do not work. For affected users, this issue can be worked around by: Manually enabling these settings by going to Settings > Accessibility > VoiceOver > Braille > Sound Curtain, or Settings > Accessibility > VoiceOver > Braille > Touch curtain respectively. For Sound Curtain, lowering the device volume to 0%. Adding the Sound Curtain to VoiceOver's Quick Settings to save a few steps. Head to Settings > Accessibility > VoiceOver > Quick Settings and select "Sound curtain." Since Touch Curtain does not have a Quick Settings option, this workaround does not apply. In Safari, the buttons to switch between the Start Page, Reading List, History, and Bookmarks do not work. It is possible to select these buttons, and VoiceOver indicates they have been selected, but the content itself does not update, meaning content cannot be reached. As a workaround, perform a one-finger triple-tap (what is known as a "long press") on the desired button to activate it. Our thanks to AppleVis user Brian Giles for this workaround. When VoiceOver focus is placed inside a text field, and then subsequently moved onto a combo box, the menu automatically opens. On occasions, when swiping through the Lock Screen using one-finger swipe right or left, VoiceOver focus may be inconsistent. When navigating through the Lock Screen using a one-finger swipe right, after the "Swipe up to Unlock" element, the expected behavior is that VoiceOver will focus on the first notification (if present); Focus status (if present); or the first item on the screen, like Flashlight or Camera. However, sometimes, VoiceOver users may find that focus is instead placed on items from the Status Bar, such as Cellular Carrier, Battery Percentage, or the Clock. If VoiceOver focus does land on items from the Status Bar when swiping, it is sometimes possible to continue swiping to the right and get to the first Lock Screen item; however, other times, VoiceOver focus can become stuck in a loop between the time, the "Swipe Up to Unlock" element, Cellular Carrier, an element with no spoken or audible feedback, or any combination of the above. Sometimes, VoiceOver does not speak the time when the device is woken with the Side Button. If this issue occurs, single-tap the screen with one finger to wake the device. After prompting Siri with the Side button, revealing the interface at the top of the screen, nothing happens when double-tapping the "Open in App" button. Double-tapping this button should work to activate it, opening the conversation in the Siri app. In the Phone App, the buttons to switch between 'All' and 'Missed' do not work. This issue can be worked around by either switching to Unified View or swiping through all calls in Classic View. Our thanks to AppleVis user Brian Giles for this workaround. Sometimes, it is not possible to access notifications with VoiceOver that are visually displayed onscreen. Typically, the 'Show notifications' button is present, but on these intermittent occasions, selecting it fails to reveal the notifications, and does nothing. If this issue occurs, double-tap and hold on the "Show Notifications" button, and swipe up. This will reveal the notifications. VoiceOver's 'Copy Speech' function copies the full semantic markup and hints, instead of just the spoken text. For example, in iOS 27, Copy Speech might paste "Latest news, heading Level 2". In previous versions of iOS, Copy Speech would only paste "Latest news," which is the desired behavior. Screen Recognition does not appear in VoiceOver's Quick Settings panel, even if selected for inclusion. The Camera App contains extraneous elements for editing Camera Controls when Edit Mode is not active. This includes "Remove" elements next to each camera control and a "Done" button that does nothing when tapped. When an app is open and VoiceOver focus is placed on the battery indicator, it is not possible to swipe to other items on the status bar. The Direct Touch option in the VoiceOver Quick Settings panel does not work. Minor Bugs In Notification Center, the Rotor Action for clearing all notifications does not work. As a workaround, Locate and double-tap on the "Clear, Notification Center" button, then double-tap on the "Confirm Clear, Notification Center" button that appears. Our thanks to AppleVis Community member Sieghard Weitzel for this workaround. On the Keypad in the Phone app, the button to place the call is labeled as "Call Answer." When focusing on a conversation in the Siri app, the Actions rotor for the conversation contains two identical "Delete" actions. When the device is set to 24-Hour Time, VoiceOver does not correctly speak the time on the top of the hour. When customising VoiceOver touch gestures and you select to replace the current command with a new one, the old command is sometimes not overwritten, necessitating manual removal and replacement. When the Safari toolbar is set to 'Bottom', the "Show Bookmarks" button is incorrectly labelled as "Bookmark." When the VoiceOver cursor reaches the first or last element onscreen in the Camera app, focus loops instead of stopping at the boundary. Improvements for VoiceOver and Braille in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 To the best of our knowledge, Apple does not routinely publish lists of bug fixes for VoiceOver or braille across releases; thus, it is difficult to get a complete accounting of every issue that has been resolved or what fixes users can expect to see upon upgrading to iOS 27 or iPadOS 27. With this in mind, our testing suggests that the following issues present in iOS/iPadOS 26 have been resolved or meaningfully improved in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27: Stability of VoiceOver focus has been significantly improved across the operating system. The screen no longer locks while VoiceOver is reading a notification on the Lock Screen. Keyboard sounds once again play when VoiceOver is on, regardless of the audio ducking setting. VoiceOver focus is no longer erratic in the App Switcher when it is opened from the Home Screen. The default volume of the Eloquence speech synthesizer more closely matches that of other voices. In Conclusion Our team has compiled lists of new vision accessibility bugs for every major iOS and iPadOS release since iOS 7 in 2013. No software from any manufacturer is completely free of bugs. That said, the number of bugs - particularly those classified as "serious" and involving core VoiceOver and braille functionality - in iOS/iPadOS 27 is deeply concerning. We call on Apple to urgently prioritize fixing the bugs listed in this post, as well as those on The AppleVis Bug Tracker . If you have not already upgraded to iOS 27 or iPadOS 27, we would strongly recommend that you take a few moments to read through any replies to this post before doing so; in case other users' experiences differ from our own. Also, consider that historically, Apple has delivered fixes for many accessibility bugs within the first few x.x.1 updates following major releases, and waiting briefly may allow Apple to resolve any initial problems reported after the public release. In the event that you do encounter an issue that is particularly bothersome, there are some troubleshooting steps you can take. Sometimes, simply toggling VoiceOver off and on again or restarting your device can resolve some issues that may arise following an OS update. Therefore, we highly recommend including these steps as part of your standard troubleshooting process. If restarting VoiceOver and/or your device does not resolve the issue, it might be worth considering a reset of your VoiceOver Settings; to do this, navigate to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Reset VoiceOver Settings. While this approach requires manually reconfiguring your customized VoiceOver settings, we have heard of multiple instances where a VoiceOver settings reset resolved issues since this feature became available in last year's iOS 26. This suggests that occasionally, problems can be attributed to local factors rather than being OS bugs. Finally, when commenting below, we ask that you please keep the discussion focused on accessibility issues specifically introduced or fixed in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27. Our release posts tend to be widely read and garner many helpful responses, so it is all the more important that readers can easily find relevant information. Also, please remember that upgrade decisions are personal, with each user's situation unique - there is no right or wrong choice. Comments criticizing others' decisions are not constructive and do nothing to add to the discussion; but they do set a negative tone and get in the way of readers finding helpful information. Furthermore, not experiencing an issue yourself does not mean that it doesn't exist for others, as bugs can be configuration-specific. Stating that an issue doesn't exist simply because you haven't encountered it is unhelpful. Our aim with these posts is to provide a forum for respectful, constructive, and honest sharing of experiences that inform decisions and empower people. In closing, we would like to again thank everyone in our community who contributed to AppleVis' testing and bug-reporting efforts during the iOS/iPadOS 27 beta cycle - be it through our Community Bug Program or just by posting on our Forum. Our information about this release is more complete because of you, and we are very grateful to all who took the time to contribute. Updates to this post Following initial publication, this post has been updated to more accurately reflect our current knowledge of iOS 27/iPadOS 27 bugs and workarounds. Specific changes include: Downgraded Sound Curtain/Touch Curtain bug from serious to moderate, and expanded on known workarounds. Added attribution of a workaround to a bug in the Phone app to Brian Giles.
en.body:
iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 were released to the public on Monday, September 14, 2026. This post contains a summary of new bugs and fixes impacting VoiceOver and Braille support that the AppleVis Editorial Team has independently validated during our use and testing of these releases.

The information contained in this post is compiled from our own use and testing of iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 during the beta period from June to September 2026; as well as from validated reports submitted by others through our Community Bug Program and shared on the AppleVis Forum. Our sincere appreciation goes to everyone who so generously took the time to share their findings with us.

At the outset, we need to state explicitly that the bug list contained in this post is not definitive and that our assessments are not infallible. While we are confident in the presence of the issues discussed in this post, there are many other reports shared on the AppleVis Forum by members of our community that we have not been able to independently replicate with the available information. Many of these reports represented use cases that are different from those of our team; and a small number were issues that, despite understanding how to reproduce them, we did not get the same results. We say all of this so that readers understand the limits of our own testing, and that others' experiences may be different from ours. An issue not being present in our bug list does not mean the issue does not exist; it simply means that we are either unaware of or unable to reproduce it.

As is our routine practice, each bug in this post has been given a severity rating. These ratings are based upon what we believe to be the implications for accessing and using features and functionality for the average user; the level of impact on the overall user experience; and whether or not there is an effective workaround for the issue. However, as these ratings are subjective to an extent, it is very possible that they may not reflect your own opinion or use case. With this in mind, we strongly recommend reading this full post and any replies before updating to iOS 27 and iPadOS 27; as we believe this will help you make an informed decision on whether to install the software at the current time or to wait for a future release. We also strongly recommend that you read this Megathread about the iOS 27 RC , as it contains a wealth of community reports about and experiences with the Release Candidate version of the software.

Some issues listed in this post and on the Forum may manifest only under specific conditions; this is all the more likely as software continues to add more features and the number of devices, available configurations, and use cases in Apple's ecosystem continues to grow. You likely will not experience every bug that we list, and you likely will not agree with every severity rating for the bugs that you do experience. While we wish it were otherwise, this is to be expected. And as is the nature with all software, it is also likely that you will encounter issues that are not reported in this post.

To ensure the information in this post is as complete and accurate as possible, we would appreciate input from those who have installed iOS 27 or iPadOS 27. Please confirm if you are encountering the same problems listed or if you have found workarounds. Please also let us know about any additional issues not mentioned here. Of course, it is even more important that you report any new bugs directly to Apple - they are already aware of the ones listed in this post. For an explanation of why and how to report bugs to Apple, see this post.

With all of the preamble out of the way, below are the new bugs for VoiceOver and Braille users which members of the AppleVis Editorial Team have personally experienced and believe to be present in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27:

In iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, there is a significant change in the sound profile of VoiceOver when the device's internal speaker is used. When compared to iOS 26, VoiceOver audio in iOS 27 has significantly less bass, particularly at lower volume levels. The resulting sound might best be described as 'neutral' or 'flat', with significantly less of the low-end emphasis and other processing that has characterized VoiceOver audio in recent versions of iOS/iPadOS.

If you have not yet upgraded to iOS 27, we believe that you can get a reasonable approximation of how VoiceOver will sound on your device by making a phone call, putting the call on speaker, and then using VoiceOver to navigate around the screen; as the flatter, more neutral sound profile that VoiceOver uses during a phone call sounds very similar to what we are hearing in iOS 27.

At the time of publication, we do not know whether the change to VoiceOver's sound profile is expected behavior; thus, we are not including it in our bug list. Nevertheless, we feel that users should be aware of this change before upgrading. If we receive additional information, we will update this post accordingly.

When the state of an item changes or the screen updates, VoiceOver does not always recognize/speak the information. This issue has many manifestations, including (but not limited to):

There is no known workaround, though VoiceOver will eventually speak the updated information if focus is moved off of and back onto the impacted element enough times.

The VoiceOver Per-Voice Equalizer (a feature that allows one to customize certain frequency/tonal characteristics of a voice) does not work. There is no known workaround. If you rely on the per-voice Equalizer, we recommend that you do not install iOS/iPadOS 27 until this issue is resolved.

To the best of our knowledge, Apple does not routinely publish lists of bug fixes for VoiceOver or braille across releases; thus, it is difficult to get a complete accounting of every issue that has been resolved or what fixes users can expect to see upon upgrading to iOS 27 or iPadOS 27. With this in mind, our testing suggests that the following issues present in iOS/iPadOS 26 have been resolved or meaningfully improved in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27:

Our team has compiled lists of new vision accessibility bugs for every major iOS and iPadOS release since iOS 7 in 2013. No software from any manufacturer is completely free of bugs. That said, the number of bugs - particularly those classified as "serious" and involving core VoiceOver and braille functionality - in iOS/iPadOS 27 is deeply concerning. We call on Apple to urgently prioritize fixing the bugs listed in this post, as well as those on The AppleVis Bug Tracker .

If you have not already upgraded to iOS 27 or iPadOS 27, we would strongly recommend that you take a few moments to read through any replies to this post before doing so; in case other users' experiences differ from our own. Also, consider that historically, Apple has delivered fixes for many accessibility bugs within the first few x.x.1 updates following major releases, and waiting briefly may allow Apple to resolve any initial problems reported after the public release.

In the event that you do encounter an issue that is particularly bothersome, there are some troubleshooting steps you can take. Sometimes, simply toggling VoiceOver off and on again or restarting your device can resolve some issues that may arise following an OS update. Therefore, we highly recommend including these steps as part of your standard troubleshooting process.

If restarting VoiceOver and/or your device does not resolve the issue, it might be worth considering a reset of your VoiceOver Settings; to do this, navigate to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Reset VoiceOver Settings. While this approach requires manually reconfiguring your customized VoiceOver settings, we have heard of multiple instances where a VoiceOver settings reset resolved issues since this feature became available in last year's iOS 26. This suggests that occasionally, problems can be attributed to local factors rather than being OS bugs.

Finally, when commenting below, we ask that you please keep the discussion focused on accessibility issues specifically introduced or fixed in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27. Our release posts tend to be widely read and garner many helpful responses, so it is all the more important that readers can easily find relevant information.

Also, please remember that upgrade decisions are personal, with each user's situation unique - there is no right or wrong choice. Comments criticizing others' decisions are not constructive and do nothing to add to the discussion; but they do set a negative tone and get in the way of readers finding helpful information. Furthermore, not experiencing an issue yourself does not mean that it doesn't exist for others, as bugs can be configuration-specific. Stating that an issue doesn't exist simply because you haven't encountered it is unhelpful. Our aim with these posts is to provide a forum for respectful, constructive, and honest sharing of experiences that inform decisions and empower people.

In closing, we would like to again thank everyone in our community who contributed to AppleVis' testing and bug-reporting efforts during the iOS/iPadOS 27 beta cycle - be it through our Community Bug Program or just by posting on our Forum. Our information about this release is more complete because of you, and we are very grateful to all who took the time to contribute.

es.title: Los nuevos modelos de Gemini apuntan a una inteligencia artificial más útil para las personas con baja visión
es.summary: Google ha presentado una nueva generación de modelos de inteligencia artificial dentro de la familia Gemini, una actualización que va mucho más allá de las mejoras técnicas para desarrolladores. Los nuevos modelos de Gemini apuntan a una inteligencia artificial más útil para las personas con baja visión, gracias a avances en velocidad, eficiencia y comprensión […] La entrada Los nuevos modelos de Gemini apuntan a una inteligencia artificial más útil para las personas con baja visión se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
Google ha presentado una nueva generación de modelos de inteligencia artificial dentro de la familia Gemini, una actualización que va mucho más allá de las mejoras técnicas para desarrolladores. Los nuevos modelos de Gemini apuntan a una inteligencia artificial más útil para las personas con baja visión , gracias a avances en velocidad, eficiencia y comprensión multimodal que pueden mejorar herramientas de accesibilidad como TalkBack, Lookout y futuros asistentes visuales integrados en Android.

Lejos de tratarse únicamente de una actualización técnica, la nueva estrategia de Google refleja una tendencia cada vez más clara: hacer que la inteligencia artificial sea capaz de comprender mejor el entorno y responder de forma casi inmediata, una característica que resulta especialmente relevante en las tecnologías de apoyo.

Entre las novedades destaca Gemini 3.6 Flash , un modelo diseñado para ofrecer respuestas más rápidas consumiendo menos recursos computacionales y reduciendo el coste de uso. Junto a él llega Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite , orientado a tareas masivas como la lectura de documentos, la clasificación de información o la traducción automática con una latencia muy baja. Google también ha presentado Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber , especializado en ciberseguridad y reservado inicialmente para organismos públicos y socios estratégicos.

Aunque estas versiones no incorporan funciones específicas de accesibilidad, sí mejoran aspectos fundamentales para quienes utilizan asistentes basados en inteligencia artificial: menor tiempo de espera, mayor capacidad para procesar imágenes y documentos y respuestas más naturales durante una conversación.

En los últimos años Google ha ido integrando Gemini en herramientas de accesibilidad como TalkBack y Lookout , dos aplicaciones ampliamente utilizadas por personas con discapacidad visual.

Gracias a estas integraciones, la inteligencia artificial ya es capaz de:

Con modelos más rápidos y eficientes, todas estas funciones pueden beneficiarse de una experiencia mucho más fluida. Si la IA tarda menos en interpretar una escena y generar una respuesta, el usuario obtiene información prácticamente en tiempo real, algo especialmente útil al desplazarse por un entorno desconocido, leer documentos extensos o identificar objetos.

Uno de los puntos fuertes de Gemini continúa siendo su capacidad multimodal, es decir, entender simultáneamente texto, imágenes, audio e incluso vídeo.

Para una persona con baja visión esto supone un cambio importante frente a los asistentes tradicionales. En lugar de limitarse a reconocer un objeto o leer un texto, la IA puede interpretar el contexto completo y responder preguntas como:

Este tipo de interacción convierte la inteligencia artificial en un auténtico asistente visual, capaz de mantener una conversación sobre lo que está viendo la cámara del dispositivo.

Otro aspecto relevante del anuncio es la reducción del consumo de tokens y del coste de procesamiento.

Aunque pueda parecer un dato dirigido únicamente a empresas, tiene una repercusión directa sobre el desarrollo de aplicaciones accesibles. Modelos más económicos permiten que desarrolladores y organizaciones sin ánimo de lucro puedan incorporar inteligencia artificial avanzada sin asumir costes tan elevados.

Esto podría favorecer la aparición de nuevas aplicaciones orientadas a la discapacidad visual, así como mejorar servicios ya existentes relacionados con la lectura inteligente, la descripción de imágenes o la navegación asistida.

La estrategia que está siguiendo Google refleja un cambio de enfoque dentro del sector de la inteligencia artificial. En lugar de centrarse únicamente en construir modelos cada vez más grandes, el objetivo pasa por desarrollar modelos especializados, rápidos y eficientes que puedan integrarse en productos reales.

Para las personas con baja visión, este enfoque resulta especialmente prometedor. La accesibilidad depende en gran medida de que las respuestas lleguen de forma inmediata y sean realmente útiles durante las actividades del día a día. Un retraso de varios segundos puede hacer que una función deje de ser práctica cuando el usuario está caminando, cruzando una calle o intentando localizar un objeto.

Aunque Google no ha presentado estas novedades como funciones específicas de accesibilidad, la evolución de Gemini puede tener un impacto significativo en las tecnologías de apoyo.

La combinación de modelos multimodales más rápidos, una integración cada vez mayor con Android y herramientas como TalkBack y Lookout, junto con una reducción de costes para desarrolladores, dibuja un escenario en el que los asistentes visuales basados en inteligencia artificial serán más precisos, rápidos y accesibles.

Todavía queda camino por recorrer, especialmente en aspectos como la fiabilidad de las descripciones o el reconocimiento en situaciones complejas. Sin embargo, la tendencia es clara: la inteligencia artificial está dejando de ser únicamente una herramienta de productividad para convertirse también en un elemento clave para mejorar la autonomía y la inclusión de las personas con discapacidad visual.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

FUENTES: El País , Google , Arxiv .

en.title: NetBoard
en.summary: NetBoard turns your computer into an instant input device for your phone, allowing you to type quickly, accurately, and effortlessly using your computer’s full physical…
en.body:
Published 14 September 2026 by Aleksandar Đurić

NetBoard turns your computer into an instant input device for your phone, allowing you to type quickly, accurately, and effortlessly using your computer’s full physical keyboard.

Built from the ground up with accessibility (A11y) as a core value, NetBoard is designed for blind, visually impaired, and motor-impaired users who find mobile touchscreen keyboards challenging to use with screen readers such as TalkBack.

Windows app: Download NetBoard for Windows .

NetBoard does not collect, log, or store your keystrokes, clipboard history, or audio files. Data is encrypted and processed strictly in transit. The app contains no ads and has no hidden fees.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

The app is fully accessible because it was developed by a blind programmer.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

Version 2.22, Android 16.

es.title: Ya disponible la segunda beta de NVDA 2026.3
es.summary: Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación, la beta 2 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, … Continuar leyendo "Ya disponible la segunda beta de NVDA 2026.3" La entrada Ya disponible la segunda beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .
es.body:
Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación , la beta 2 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, o por el sistema de informe de fallos de NV Access . Esta versión no es apta para entornos de producción. Al instalar esta beta te unirás al canal beta, y sólo recibirás avisos de actualización de compilaciones beta y candidatas a liberación (rc). El canal beta/rc siempre te mantendrá al día con la versión más reciente de NVDA. La última rc de un ciclo de liberación es idéntica a la última versión estable. Para regresar al canal de versiones estables, instala a mano la última versión estable.

Esta versión incorpora importantes mejoras de rendimiento, mejoras en los diálogos de NVDA, y entrada expandida por la pantalla táctil. Se han hecho varias mejoras para reducir los retrasos y aumentar el rendimiento. Ahora NVDA recupera y captura más información sobre los controles en segundo plano, mejorando el rendimiento en controles como cuadros combinados y el explorador de archivos. NVDA ya no hace que se rompan el explorador de archivos u otras aplicaciones al cerrarlo o reiniciarlo. NVDA se recupera ahora más rápido cuando una aplicación deja de responder, y ya no se colgará ni inundará el registro con errores en aplicaciones que no responden. En regiones vivas de texto, como las terminales, NVDA ya no se cuelga cuando se vuelcan en pantalla importantes cantidades de texto. Se han añadido menús de contexto y atajos de teclado a los diálogos de perfiles de configuración, gestos de entrada y diccionarios del habla, haciendo que estos diálogos sean más fáciles de usar con el teclado. Ahora también es posible cambiar directamente un gesto existente en el diálogo Gestos de entrada. Se ha modernizado el diálogo que presenta mensajes explorables y ahora soporta mejor cambiar su tamaño, maximizarlo y minimizarlo. Se ha expandido significativamente la entrada por pantalla táctil. Los gestos de dos deslizamientos secuenciales ahora combinan dos deslizamientos en rápida sucesión en un solo gesto, incrementando enormemente la cantidad de gestos asociables. También se soportan ahora los gestos de borde, permitiendo que los gestos que comiencen a 15 mm de cualquier borde de la pantalla se asocien independientemente de los mismos gestos realizados en el centro de la pantalla. Se ha añadido una nueva orden sin asignar para mover el cursor del ratón al centro de la vista ampliada. Se puede usar el OCR de Windows con la lupa o la cortina de pantalla activadas. Se ha actualizado Liblouis con nuevas tablas braille en Elfdaliano, sami, maorí, braille unificado inglés de Nueva Zelanda, y aitiano criollo, una tabla noruega para texto en español, y variantes adicionales de sueco de 6 y 8 puntos. Se ha actualizado Espeak NG añadiendo soporte para liguriano y abkhaz. Para instalar esta beta, puedes configurar el canal «rc y beta» en el complemento Selector del canal de actualización y buscar actualizaciones desde el menú Ayuda de NVDA, o actualizar desde una beta anterior. Y como siempre, también puedes descargar manualmente el instalador de NVDA 2026.3 beta 2 . Su suma de comprobación SHA256, que te permitirá garantizar la integridad del archivo descargado, es d26386e7ac3ac6d245c8adcfc82c07e9332278360af3396b69888b6b31e08d33. ¡Feliz lunes!

La entrada Ya disponible la segunda beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .

en.title: Brainclash
en.summary: New here? Challenge a friend, answer whenever you wish, and let the sharpest mind win. Multiple categories, and a daily reward waiting for you. Brainclash is a quiz game with a different rhythm: a refined battle of minds you take on in your own time, with no pressure. Challenge a friend to a match, let the game pair you with a random opponent, or train first against the computer. Play unfolds turn by turn: you answer, then your opponent answers, and the most accurate one wins. There's no tense timer forcing you both online at the same moment — take your turn whenever you like, and return for the next one anytime. Questions span a wide range of categories — General Knowledge, Science & Nature, History, Geography, Sports, and Arts & Entertainment — so you'll always find something that suits your interests and adds to what you know. And when a hard question comes your way, you have tools to help: remove half the options with 50:50, swap a question that doesn't suit you, or grant yourself a few extra seconds. The more you win, the higher you climb through the levels and the more coins you collect — and each day you can spin the daily wheel for a free reward. The game is made for everyone to enjoy: it works smoothly with TalkBack and VoiceOver, so screen reader users get a complete experience, crafted to be heard and not only seen. Add your friends, exchange messages between matches, and discover together who deserves the title of the smartest. Play in Arabic or English, and switch languages whenever you wish. So, are you ready to compete? Your next opponent is waiting on your move. Heading

en.title: What's new in Accessibility in iOS 27 for Blind and DeafBlind Users
en.summary: Introduction 15 years ago, I produced my first "What's New in iOS Accessibility" article. Every September since, I've been documenting what my testing of the betas has yielded. There are many welcome mainstream changes in this year's iOS 27, such as the upgraded Siri app, new parental controls, a slider to adjust Liquid Glass, further enhanced Apple Intelligence features, and much more. The new Siri has its own app, and coverage of it is beyond the scope of this article other than to mention it's much more versatile and can assist with all kinds of tasks from asking about your personal data to recipes and so on. Lots of individuals will be reviewing these new features. As I've done for many years now, I'm documenting my findings after testing the new version of iOS throughout the summer to discuss accessibility-specific features which impact blind and DeafBlind users. Following what has become a tradition, Apple began discussing enhancements coming to accessibility with its announcement ahead of Global Accessibility Awareness Day. More info about forthcoming features was detailed during the Worldwide Developers Conference Keynote. Devices that will work with iOS 27, according to Apple, are the iPhone SE 2 and later, as well as the iPhone 11 and later. The page linked to above is also a good resource for mainstream changes coming in iOS 27. VoiceOver Though there are fewer changes in iOS 27 than what were found in iOS 26, VoiceOver has gained quite a bit of new functionality. Whether you are a speech user or a braille one, there are a lot of new offerings in this year's release. Pronounce It Together There is now a setting which allows a VoiceOver user to import or share their pronunciation dictionary. This feature could be helpful when, for example, text-to-speech engines do not pronounce things correctly in local dialects. Instead of everyone having to make the changes, one person could compile it and share it with other users in a similar situation. It could also be used as a form of prank. Imagine changing the pronunciation of a friend's name to a friendly insult along with other changes and they later encounter it. These settings can be found under Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Speech> Pronunciations. Selecting 'Import' will bring up the Files function and allow the user to browse to the file they wish to import. Sharing one's own pronunciations brings up the standard Share Sheet, where the file can be sent to any number of places or contacts. Hide Your Cursor For those who may not be aware, the VoiceOver cursor appears as a black rectangular outline surrounding the item that currently has VoiceOver focus. While handy in some situations such as showing a sighted user where VoiceOver focus is set, helping a low vision user who tracks VoiceOver focus, or when demonstrating VoiceOver support to a developer, there are certainly reasons individuals may wish to disable it. This is because it can also serve as a distraction when the VoiceOver cursor itself isn't an important part of the iPhone's purpose. For example, when using the iPhone for face-to-face communication as a DeafBlind user, it can distract the person you are attempting to communicate with from the text you are typing. Some may wish to hide the visual VoiceOver cursor during screen sharing. To adjust this setting, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Cursor Visibility, and choose from showing the cursor, hiding it always, or hiding it during screen sharing. Navigating in New Ways with Explore By Touch iOS 27 brings new options to precisely control VoiceOver's reading of text when using Explore by Touch, or, as it's more commonly referred to, 'dragging your finger around the screen'. Options for Text Exploration are now Paragraph, Line, or Sentence. For example, when set to 'Sentence', VoiceOver will only speak the sentence under your finger instead of the entire element as it previously did. Users can adjust this by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Text Exploration. Note that changes made in Text Exploration only apply to Explore by Touch, and will not impact swiping through content. At least, not this particular setting. It's for Swipers Too A separate setting, called Text Navigation, offers the ability to modify how VoiceOver moves when swiping left and right through the screen with one finger. The available options are Line, Sentence, Paragraph, and Element. In addition to allowing one to more easily read blocks of text that VoiceOver sees as one large element, having these two new sets of options can give VoiceOver users other choices than the rotor for text navigation. To check out the new settings for swiping, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Text Navigation. Remember that you will need to adjust settings for Text Exploration and Text Navigation separately. Hints Become Customizable For a lot of the clients I work with who use speech, the hints offered by VoiceOver can be helpful, but there comes a point where they cause interference with touchscreen navigation once a user advances in their journey of learning VoiceOver. For example, "Double Tap to Open" can grind on one's nerves after a while. When I first started learning to use an iPhone with iOS 4, this was also something I became frustrated with. If the system hints become a nuisance, the user now has more control over them. iOS 27 brings the ability to adjust the amount of delay between when VoiceOver provides active information about what is in focus and when the hint will be conveyed. To configure this, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Verbosity> Hints, and then either type the duration in seconds ranging from 0.05 to 2.0, or use the 'Decrement' and 'Increment' buttons. The default is 0.8 seconds. It's also now possible to specify if users want all hints, app-specific hints, or no hints at all. You can find these options on the same screen. No Modifier Required for These Functions For VoiceOver commands to be assigned to keyboard shortcuts, Bluetooth keyboard users have always had to include their chosen VoiceOver modifier along with the command. This is no longer necessary with the function keys located in the top row of many Bluetooth keyboards. The setting must be enabled, which one can do by going to Settings>Accessibility>VoiceOver>Commands and setting the Switch Button for "No Modifier Keys" to on. Instead of having to press, for example, VoiceOver Modifier f8 to launch the VoiceOver Settings menu, users can now simply press F8. Live and Open for Questions Live Recognition was first integrated into VoiceOver with iOS 18. iOS 27, coupled with Apple Intelligence, gives Live Recognition even more power. Activating the 'Ask' button will allow the user to ask about what is currently in the camera's view. It's also possible to tell Live Recognition to focus on a specific thing in your environment. As long as that item is able to be tracked, its actions and movements will often be reported by VoiceOver. Ask is a feature that is highly customizable. Going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Live Recognition allows the user to set up some other options. One can change the default question asked when the button is activated, make the default input either dictation or typing, and have the Volume buttons take a still photo for a follow-up or more detailed description. Ask can be set up with a gesture, Bluetooth keyboard command, the Accessibility Shortcut, or a Perkins-style keyboard command. If none of those are what the user wants, there is also the ability to launch the Ask feature using the Action Button. It can be enabled by going to Settings> Action Button, selecting the Accessibility category, and then choosing 'Ask a Question'. The View From iOS In my view, pardon the pun, the largest upgrade for VoiceOver and braille users in iOS 27 is the massive overhaul of the Image Recognition feature. This is thanks to Apple Intelligence, but I'm sure those using iPhone 15 and earlier devices aren't feeling very thankful, since they do not have access to these features. Unlike the multi-step processes involved with using third-party services for detailed descriptions, Image Recognition descriptions typically take less than three seconds. They can be generated on virtually all images the iPhone encounters, and the user does not need to download or upload each image they wish to have described. It is also possible to describe the screen of the device itself, to ask questions about the image in focus, and to generate a description with the ability to ask a follow-up question immediately. These features can be activated through the VoiceOver rotor or by adding specific functions to gestures. The two devices I have upgraded at this point had the Image Recognition options in the Rotor. If, by chance, your Rotor does not have the Image Recognition option after upgrading, it can be added by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Rotor> Rotor Items and selecting Image Recognition. Since there are up to seven different options for Image Recognition, Apple has also given users the ability to add and remove what they wish to this rotor item. It can be configured by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Rotor> Image Recognition Rotor. Each of the available options will be discussed below. Image/Item Description will allow the user to get a description of the image or item that VoiceOver focus is set to. Based on my testing, it is generated in less than three seconds. It will be delivered in the form of a VoiceOver announcement. For those using braille, one can read the description at their own pace by pressing Space with N. When done, pressing space with n will return the user to where they were before. Further, there were some issues in iOS 26 with cursor routing buttons not routing correctly and focus jumping back to the top in longer blocks of text while the user was reading. I also encourage users to check out the AppleVis list of bugs and fixes. If needed, more information on how to update the software on your device is available on this Apple Support page. T

Lots of individuals will be reviewing these new features. Devices that will work with iOS 27, according to Apple, are the iPhone SE 2 and later, as well as the iPhone 11 and later. Though there are fewer changes in iOS 27 than what were found in iOS 26, VoiceOver has gained quite a bit of new functionality. Whether you are a speech user or a braille one, there are a lot of new offerings in this year's release.

These settings can be found under Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Speech> Pronunciations. en.title: ‎Muse from Meta
en.summary: Muse is a personal AI agent that can manage email and schedules, book reservations, track spending, compare prices, plan workouts, and handle multistep tasks. It can connect to apps you choose, keep working after you close it, and ask for approval before taking actions. You can interact with Muse either through the native iOS app, through a browser interface at http://muse.ai or through WhatsApp chat messages. Includes a robust free tier, and optional paid subscriptions if you go over.

en.title: YugoSoft Messages
en.summary: YugoSoft Messages is a modern, fast, and fully accessible SMS application, built with the vision of making messaging easy and barrier-free for everyone. The app…
en.body:
YugoSoft Messages is a modern, fast, and fully accessible SMS application, built with the vision of making messaging easy and barrier-free for everyone.

The app was designed from the ground up in close collaboration with blind and visually impaired users, making it fully optimized for screen readers like TalkBack. Custom TalkBack Actions allow you to delete messages, block senders, or mark conversations as read with a single swipe and double-tap, offering a level of convenience and accessibility that goes beyond mainstream messaging apps.

In addition to strong accessibility, YugoSoft Messages includes advanced features that make it suitable as a daily messaging app for any user.

Try YugoSoft Messages and experience SMS communication that is simple, fast, and truly accessible to all.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

The app is completely accessible and supports screen reader actions.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

Version 1.61, tested on Android 15 and 16.

en.title: Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK)
en.summary: Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK) is an Android keyboard for blind and low-vision users. Refined over many years together with blind users, it was rebuilt from…
en.body:
Published 13 September 2026 by Philip Heyse

Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK) is an Android keyboard for blind and low-vision users. Refined over many years together with blind users, it was rebuilt from the ground up in summer 2026: modern, faster, and adjustable in great detail.

Two ways to type, both letting you check a key before it is sent:

– Lift to Type: slide your finger over the keys, hear each one, and commit by lifting it – Double Tap to Type: the first tap reads the key, a second tap confirms it

1. Setup and settings:

Setup is guided step by step and confirms out loud when the keyboard is enabled and selected.

The settings screen is made for TalkBack: a switch and its label are read as one element, and sections announced with a “Section:” prefix.

Settings can be saved to a file and restored later. A session log can be exported or e-mailed if you need help.

2. Keyboard layouts:

264 layouts are included. For most languages you can choose between Simple (four rows), Fluent Flow (five rows with numbers), Fluent Flow with Cursor (plus cursor keys), PC (Ctrl, Alt and function keys), PC with Num Pad, and Robo Gear (familiar from standard smartphone keyboards).

Hold the space bar for the Quick Menu to switch layouts. The full list of languages is at the end of this text.

The app itself is translated into 30 languages, including Finnish, Malay and Urdu.

3. What you hear:

– Adjustable speed and pitch, with upper and lower case told apart by pitch – Choice of speech engine, with language, country and voice – Optional NATO alphabet, so “B” and “D” are never confused – Spoken names for punctuation, symbols and emoji – Announcements when the keyboard opens or closes, when you move between letters, numbers, symbols and emoji, and on Shift, Alt or Ctrl changes – Key click sounds in three styles, with adjustable volume – Vibration when typing and on gestures, each switchable separately

4. Voice input:

Start dictation with the microphone key or the Quick Menu, and choose between:

– Your device’s own dictation – A model running on your device: no account needed, works offline, though less accurate than the online options – Popular AI services, using your own API key, stored encrypted on your device only

5. Typing support:

– Auto-correct for many of the supported languages. One Backspace restores the original word. Never runs in password fields. – Text shortcuts: “brt” becomes “Best regards, Tom”. One Backspace undoes it. – Clipboard history above the keys. Tap an entry to insert it. – Your own keys for text you often need, such as your e-mail address – Optional capital letter at the start of a sentence – Adjustable delay and repeat speed when holding Delete or Backspace

6. Subscription:

BAK is funded by a small subscription. It costs less than the equivalent of one US dollar per month, and follows the local price level, so in many countries it is lower. It pays for ongoing work: fixing bugs, keeping up with new Android versions, and adding features. Before subscribing, you can try the keyboard in the test field on the app’s home screen. A subscription is needed to use it in other apps.

7. Help and contact: – https://bright-side.de/bak/ – ba * @ ********* de.de

The Help section in the app has the documentation, the mailing list, and a way to e-mail the developer.

8. Layouts for your language:

Arabic (also with French), Belarusian, Bengali, Bulgarian (Cyrillic, Latin, Phonetic), Canadian (also French, Multilingual), Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English (UK, USA), French (France, Switzerland), German (Germany, Switzerland), Greek, Gujarati, Hebrew, Hindi (also InScript), Hungarian, Indonesian, Italian (Italy, Switzerland), Kannada, Marathi, Norwegian, Persian, Polish (also programmer), Portuguese (also Brazilian ABNT), Punjabi, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Spanish (Spain, Latin America), Swedish, Tamil, Telugu, Turkish (F and Q), Ukrainian, Vietnamese.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

The keyboard app was specifically designed for blind or visually impaired users.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

5.0.7

en.title: Final Fortress
en.summary: Final Fortress is a match-3 puzzle. The whole game is the screen of an old terminal: green text, one cursor, and you, the commandant of the last fortress. It is a quiet game. A working console in the dark, the hum of the systems, static like rain. A watch takes fifteen or twenty minutes: do the day's tasks, read what came in, hand over. Nothing hurries you, and nothing happens while you are away. Come back after a week and the fortress is exactly as you left it. Match tiles to finish the day's tasks. Each task brings supplies. Spend them to repair the fortress: reactor, hydroponics, antenna, armory, infirmary. Every repaired system opens new missions. Match 4 or more to charge special tiles. They clear a line, a block, or every tile of one kind. Swap two charged tiles together and they fire as one bigger shape, up to the whole board. The board gets busier as you go: convoy crates that pay out at the bottom, sealed containers with a special tile inside, interference to clear layer by layer, burned sectors the tiles fall past. Some tasks ask for a pattern: decode a sequence in order, or fill a gauge in every column. AI Madness is a mode of its own, outside the fortress. Each shift bends the rules: boards up to 10 by 13, sometimes only three kinds of tile, cascades that barely stop, tasks that may be impossible. On an iPhone with Apple Intelligence, Apple's on-device model (Foundation Models) picks the shift's character and writes its line in the log. Nothing leaves the phone. Otherwise the terminal does the same on its own. Nothing is at stake and nothing is banked. Every shift has a code. Send it to a friend and they get exactly the same board. There is a story in the log: three acts, four threads, and the notes of the commandants who held the fortress before you. It comes a few lines at a time. Read it or skip it. The game never nags about it. Repair the antenna and you will see a board with other players' stations. It is view-only, there is no chat, and it updates once a day. When the story is over, the log keeps going quietly on its own. The music belongs to your fortress alone. The sound is synthesized live and seeded from your fortress, so your station hums like no other and never loops. The hum changes with what is running, with the hour of the night and with the weather outside. Each kind of tile has its own note, and a cascade climbs the scale. One extra room, The Long Dark, carries a call of its own. Three more stations use the instruments in your phone: a weather post that reads the barometer, an acoustic modem and a direction finder. A home screen widget shows your fortress at a glance, in StandBy too. No ads. No lives, timers, energy or streaks. No pop-ups, no push notifications, no accounts, no daily rewards to come back for. Run out of moves and the terminal just says the packet was lost. Try again, nothing is taken away. You can drop a task at any time. Purchases are cosmetic only: screen colors, one extra soundtrack, custom names. Nothing you can buy helps you play, and no purchase moves you up the board. Works offline, on iPhone and iPad. Fully playable with VoiceOver, with a flicker-free stable phosphor mode and a calm mode that softens the board's flashes and haptics.

en.title: One Line Journal app
en.summary: One sentence a day. One book at the end of the year. Your life is happening — quietly, quickly, in small moments. One Line, One Year captures 2026 as it unfolds and turns it into a beautifully structured book that's entirely yours. HOW IT WORKS Daily — Write one sentence about your day. That's it. Weekly — Once a week, reflect in 3–5 sentences. Your daily entries appear above for context, so nothing gets lost. Monthly — Write a brief summary that becomes a full chapter in your book. Book View — Watch your year assemble itself in real time — months as chapters, weeks and days woven beneath them. Export — At year's end, export your complete book as Markdown, PDF, or DOCX. BUILT FOR PRIVACY Everything stays on your device. No accounts. No cloud sync. No analytics. Face ID and passcode lock keep your words yours — and auto-lock kicks in the moment you leave the app. THOUGHTFUL DETAILS Highlights to mark the moments worth remembering Tags to thread themes across your year Gentle reminders to keep the habit alive A clean, distraction-free writing interface Simple timeline navigation — no clutter, no feed NO SOCIAL. NO NOTIFICATIONS. NO NOISE. Just you and your words, building something you'll want to read. A year feels long while you're living it. It feels short when you look back. Capture it — one sentence at a time.
